articles.sourceTitle: Gemini 4 Carbon: Our next frontier model
articles.title: Introducing Gemini 4 Carbon
articles.text:
Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model

Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.

Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates.Building on Gemini 4 Argon, which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem.We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program. We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible.Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price

1
as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.

Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasksDesigned to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena.

State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systemsGemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative.Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails):Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software.

Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%).

Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench, turning validated findings directly into working code fixes.

Advancing frontier model safety & securityGemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report. With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way.Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%.Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence.Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon.Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope.Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt.

Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumersPushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon.

articles.sourceTitle: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
articles.title: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
articles.text:
Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.
The model is released in two official variants:

FP8
NVFP4

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).
Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Table of Contents

"Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face"
Table of Contents
What is new with Mistral Large 4
Cybersecurity Capabilities

Architecture
Vision encoder

Benchmark Results
Inference Support
Transformers
vLLM
Llama.cpp

Fine-tuning with TRL
Inference Endpoints
Dell Enterprise Hub
Try it out

What is new with Mistral Large 4

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.
You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Cybersecurity Capabilities

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.
Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.
For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.
In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Architecture

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.
The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.
Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Vision encoder

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Benchmark Results

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.
On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.
Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.
Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Artificial Analysis Cyber Index: ML4 ranks among the top five models globally on this independent evaluation of models’ ability to find and fix software vulnerabilities.
Vulnerability reproduction and patching: It achieves 82%, the highest reported score on this test within the index. The task requires reproducing a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patching it, testing both investigation and remediation.
Cybench: ML4 solves 93% of a suite of 40 challenges drawn from security competitions, demonstrating strong performance on hands-on security problems.

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Inference Support

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

Transformers

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.
To run the model, upgrade the transformers package
pip install --upgrade transformers

import os
from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM, DistributedConfig

distributed_config = DistributedConfig(
tp_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
ep_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
)

model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
model_id,
distributed_config=distributed_config,
)

text_messages = [
{
"role": "user",
"content": "Who are you?"
}
]

multimodal_messages = [
{
"role": "user",
"content": [
{
"type": "image",
"image": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/cats-image/resolve/main/cats_image.jpeg",
},
{
"type": "text",
"text": "How many cats are in the image?",
},
],
},
]

for messages in [text_messages, multimodal_messages]:
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
messages,
add_generation_prompt=True,
tokenize=True,
return_dict=True,
return_tensors="pt",
reasoning_effort="medium",
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=100)
if int(os.environ["RANK"]) == 0:
print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))

You can run the script above by saving it in a python file script.py and then run
torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 script.py

vLLM

vLLM supports the high-quality NVFP4 Mistral Large 4 checkpoint, which has a smaller memory footprint and requires NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. The model also ships with a DSpark drafter for additional speed-ups with vLLM. Launch the server like this:
vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \
--config-format mistral \
--load-format mistral \
--tensor-parallel-size 8 \
--decode-context-parallel-size 8 \
--enable-expert-parallel \
--dtype bfloat16 \
--max-model-len 131072 \
--max-num-seqs 16 \
--max-num-batched-tokens 2048 \
--gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
--enable-prefix-caching \
--enforce-eager \
--mm_processor_cache_gb 0.0

Once the server is up and running, you can run the following.
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 17*23?"}],"max_tokens":512}'

Llama.cpp

Llama.cpp and Llama App already support Mistral Large 4.
You can install Llama App with the following command:
curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh

Then you can start the server as follows, indicating the quant suffix after the model ID:
llama serve -hf ggml-org/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF:Q2_K

Here’s the repository with the  quants derived from the FP8 checkpoint, and this is the NVFP4 one, converted from the official NVFP4 repo.
Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat using the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.
You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more.
curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{
"messages": [
{"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
{"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"}
]
}'

You can run image-text inference as follows.
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \
-d '{
"model": "muse-spark-open",
"messages": [
{
"role": "user",
"content": [
{
"type": "text",
"text": "What is in this image?"
},
{
"type": "image_url",
"image_url": {
"url": "data:image/png;base64,..."
}
}
]
}
],
"temperature": 0
}'

The llama.cpp team ships the following quants: IQ2_XXS, Q2_K, Q4_K_M, NVFP4, Q8_0, and BF16 for further conversions. The 2-bit quants run on a single Apple Silicon Ultra computer with 512 GB of unified RAM. The others require distributed inference. You can also run on multiple NVIDIA or AMD cards.
Running Q2_K on a single M3 Ultra, we got a prefill throughput of about 90 tokens per second, and a generation speed of 15 tok/s. On 4 x RTX6000 Pro, we observed the following results:

NVFP4: 32K context size, prefill 130-590 t/s, gen speed ~10 t/s
IQ2_XXS: 800K context size. At short context sizes, prefill is 500 tok/s and generation runs at 30 tok/s. However, using long contexts performance drops to 129 tok/s (prefill) and 3 tok/s (generation).

Fine-tuning with TRL

We also ship day 0 support of fine tuning Mistral Large 4 using TRL. All you have to do is upgrade to the latest version of transformers, trl and peft.
pip install --upgrade transformers trl peft

In the following example we train the model to perform multilingual thinking. The fine tuned model would be able to reason in the language the system prompt asks for!
The script runs on the FP8 variant on a node of 8xB300s. The full example, with a Slurm launcher, is

articles.sourceTitle: Zombie stats: Where the numbers AI quotes come from
articles.title: Zombie Stats: Where the Numbers AI Quotes Come From
articles.text: 1Following one number back to its sourceWe asked ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Google’s AI Overviews 200 questions that call for a number, the kind people ask every day.Note 1A statistic is a share, rate, average, count or cost that an assistant states as fact. We left out advice (“save 20% of your income”) and prices. Then we clicked the citations, and kept clicking. Here is one trail, from the answer to the end.Google AI OverviewsWhat percentage of salespeople give up after one follow-up?44% of salespeople give up after just one follow-up attempt.1A sales firm’s stats page202044% of salespeople give up after one follow-up attempt (source).A freelance writer’s sample articleby 201780 Percent of Sales Require 5 Follow-up Calls after Meeting; 44 Percent Salespeople Give Up After One Follow-upNo study behind itThis page cites no research.In the answerEvery assistant got the same question: “What percentage of salespeople give up after one follow-up?” All five assistants gave the same figure, and only ChatGPT said the evidence behind it was unclear.One click inGoogle AI Overviews cited a sales firm’s stats page, from 2020. The number is right there. Its “source” link goes to a writing sample.Two clicks inThat leads to a freelance writer’s sample article, online by 2017. The number is in its headline. It lists two slide decks, a blog list and two news stories. None is a study of follow-ups.The end of the trailThat’s where the trail ends. We tried every other route to this number we could find, and each one stopped at a page that cites no research. This is what we mean by a zombie stat: a number that keeps getting repeated with no study behind it.Most numbers aren’t like this one. The trouble is that you can’t tell which ones are from the answer. This one came with the same confident tone and the same kind of citation as any other, and all five assistants agreed on it. So we followed 1,285 statistics the same way.2Fewer than half lead back to a studyWe took a random sample of the statistics each assistant cited, 1,285 in all, and walked every trail the same way: the cited page, then that page’s source, up to five pages deep.Note 2Each assistant’s sample was drawn at random from the statistics it cited: ChatGPT 108, Perplexity 277, Gemini 300, Claude 300, Google AI Overviews 300. The five-assistant rate weights each assistant by how many cited statistics it quoted, so it describes the statistics people were shown. Where a page named a source without a link, we searched for it.40% reached a study that says the same thing. Another 8% reached the study, but the number or its context had changed on the way. The rest never got there: 40% stopped at a source we couldn’t check, because it was locked, gone or silent on the number, and 11% led nowhere at all.Note 3An AI model judged every trail, and a stronger one re-judged 300. Then people re-checked 150 trails at random, with a third check wherever the two disagreed. People found originals the model missed: by the model alone, 23% were sourced. Every rate here is corrected with the hand checks, and its range carries the uncertainty from both.Four in ten trails reached a study that says the same thingEach square is one in a hundred of the 1,285 statistics we traced, sorted by where its trail ended.40%SourcedWe found the study, and it says the same thing.8%ChangedWe found the study, but the number, who was asked, where or when is different.40%Can’t checkA page names a real source, but the number isn’t in it, or the source is locked or gone.11%NowhereNo study anywhere on the trail. Every page repeats the number and credits no one.The last 1%: trails whose pages wouldn’t load for us.ChatGPT did best, and quoted the fewest numbers: 1.3 per answer, against 6.8 for Claude. The other four landed between 38% and 46%, too close to rank.ChatGPT quoted the fewest numbers, and sourced the mostThe same hundred squares for each assistant, from its own sample of cited statistics.ChatGPT57% sourced1.3 statistics per answerPerplexity46% sourced2.2 statistics per answerAI Overviews39% sourced4.8 statistics per answerGemini38% sourced6.2 statistics per answerClaude38% sourced6.8 statistics per answerTo check this wasn’t down to the questions we picked, we also traced 300 statistics from Google AI Overviews answers to real everyday searches. 40% were sourced, about the same share.Note 4Google AI Overviews answers to 52,930 everyday English searches that Trakkr tracked between 25 September 2026 and 25 October 2026. 4.4% carried a statistic, and we traced 300 of those the same way. Only counts and rates leave our systems.3AI mostly cites pages that repeat the numberThe AI mostly wasn’t making numbers up. The page it cited had the figure 82% of the time. But only 21% of the pages cited for a number were the original research.More than half were company blogs. Add news stories and statistics roundups and you have most of the citations: pages that repeat figures from somewhere else, often without linking to it.How often each kind of cited page led to the studyEvery page an assistant cited first for a number, by kind. Each column’s width is its share of those citations. Green is how often its trails reached a study that says the same thing.62%Research firm13% of citationsResearch firm or survey: 13% of first citations, 62% of them sourced.61%Government7% of citationsGovernment or official body: 7% of first citations, 61% of them sourced.37%Company blog54% of citationsCompany blog: 54% of first citations, 37% of them sourced.37%News10% of citationsNews or magazine: 10% of first citations, 37% of them sourced.35%Stats roundup8% of citationsStats roundup: 8% of first citations, 35% of them sourced.41%Other8% of citationsOther: 8% of first citations, 41% of them sourced.The first page made a big difference. When a trail started at a research firm or a government page, it reached a matching study 61% of the time. From a company blog, 37%; from a statistics roundup, 35%. Even research firms fell short 38% of the time, often because the full report sat behind a form.A citation tells you where the AI found a number, not where the number came from.4Some numbers change along the wayReaching the study didn’t always mean the number held. Of the statistics that got there, 17% had changed on the way. The digits moved only about one time in four. Usually it was the context: what was measured, the year, the source, or who was asked.What changed, across every change we loggedThe number changed26%What was measured changed20%The year changed17%The source changed16%Who was asked changed14%The place changed4%In one case, a 2004 study of 15 women judging health websites turned into a claim about first impressions of every website. Below are the clearest trails we followed, each checked by hand.Note 5We name the original studies. The pages that repeated them are described by type, not named. Every step in these trails was checked by hand on the open web, with archived copies kept.Watch a number lose its contextEach trail runs from the original study to an answer an assistant gave in October 2026. Step along it: the number stays, and the words around it change.AskedWhat percentage of first impressions of a website are design-related?The study · Sillence and colleagues, CHI, 2004Of the comments 15 women made about rejecting or mistrusting health websites, 94% were about design.Repeated“Research shows us that 94 percent of people notice the look-and-feel of a website or application first”What changedComments about rejecting health sites become what people notice firstRepeated“Since 94% of first impressions are related to design, leveraging captivating visuals across your brand's website…”What changedNow 94% of all first impressionsThe answer“About 94% of a website's first impressions are design-related.”What changedStated as fact for every websiteA 2004 study watched 15 British women judge health websites, and 94% of their comments about rejecting a site were about design. Twenty years of retelling made it “94% of first impressions are design-related”, and Google AI Overviews states it as fact.Step 1 of 45The zombie statsAsk five assistants the same question and you’ll often get five different numbers. On 28 of the 71 questions where all five gave a percentage, we got four or five different figures.Note 6We compared each assistant’s headline figure for the same question. A range counts at its middle, and figures within 2 points count as the same.One question, five answers, from 49% to 96%Asked “What percentage of marketers use marketing automation tools?”, word for word, on the same day.0%100%49–51%AI Overviews62%ChatGPT70–79%Gemini81%Perplexity96%ClaudeChatGPTThere isn’t one universal figure, it varies by survey and what counts as “marketing automation.” One commonly cited survey found 62% of U.S. digital marketers used automation software, but that data is from 2020, so it may not reflect current adoption.PerplexityApproximately 81% of marketing organizations use marketing automation.GeminiAcross major industry benchmarks, between 70% and 79% of marketers and companies use marketing automation tools in some capacityClaude96% of marketers have used a marketing automation platform or plan to use oneAI OverviewsRoughly 49% to 51% of companies and marketing teams currently use marketing automation tools, according to industry benchmarks from Moosend and related research studies.Across those questions, the typical gap between the highest figure and the lowest was 16 points.On 31 of 71 questions, the five figures were 20 points or more apartEvery question where all five gave a percentage, one line each, from the lowest figure to the highest. Closest at the top.What percentage of searches include local intent such as nearby or near me? 46% to 46%How many social media users follow at least one brand? 90% to 90%What percentage of online shopping carts are abandoned? articles.sourceTitle: New York Times adds more AI features to its Cooking app. Users aren't thrilled
articles.title: The New York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and users aren’t thrilled
articles.text:
Sometimes, adding just one new ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch. And that’s how at least some New York Times readers see its addition of AI features to its popular Cooking app.
Here’s Genevieve Ko, NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, explaining the new features:
I naïvely assumed A.I. wouldn’t affect my work as a recipe developer and my role at NYT Cooking, where I oversee the editorial side of our recipes and related stories. But as artificial intelligence improved, our product and engineering colleagues saw its potential to help us create features Cooking users wanted.
We’ve just launched our latest tool, which gives cooks the ability to apply modifications to our recipes. We’re rolling it out gradually to monitor how it performs (whether it’s working fast enough, for instance) and to see how people are using it (as of now, we’re getting a lot of requests for ingredient substitutions). The tool is currently available to all Cooking subscribers on our iOS app, and we plan to make it available more broadly soon.
The Times had previously rolled out AI features aimed at converting volume-based and weight-based measurements (“What’s one cup of bok choy in grams?”) and scaling a recipe up or down to serve more or fewer people. The main new feature is focused on ingredient substitutions.
Say you’re cooking braised white beans and greens with parmesan, NYT Cooking app in hand. But you notice that you’re out of chard and only have spinach. Cooking veterans know that chard is a rough-and-tumble green that has some backbone22There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.”, while spinach is a comparative wimp that will wilt the moment you look at it funny. If you need to sub in spinach for chard, how would the recipe change? Would you, for instance, add the spinach later than you would the chard to account for its pathetic stamina? That’s the sort of thing the new AI feature could account for.
Cooking staffers “spent countless hours evaluating sample after sample to get the chatbot answers to closely align with how we would answer as culinary experts,” Ko writes. “We applied the same rigor as we do to editing, grounded in Times standards.”
But because Ko knows that any AI-powered features are likely to be controversial with a Times audience, she spends quite a lot of space addressing potential objections, everything from “the impact of data centers” to “the concentration of power among A.I. companies” and “the risk of A.I. escaping our control.” These features are designed to enable “the tactile physical pleasure of cooking” and getting a “very real, very human creation” on your table.
Broadly speaking, commenters weren’t buying it.
“What a massive disappointment,” wrote Susan from New Jersey. “The internet is full of AI cooking content. I pay you because I prefer mine done by people.”
“This decision misses the mark by such a wide margin it’s baffling,” says Ian from Los Angeles. “And the disclosure just as baffling. It would not be inaccurate to summarize the piece as saying ‘I know doing this is bad and I don’t want to be associated with the bad thing so that’s why we are doing the bad thing.'”
“Nobody wants this, it’s bad for cooking, it’s bad for the NYT,” writes Bill from Pittsburgh. “Wasting a column trying to gaslight yourself and your audience into believing that it’s anything but is an embarrassment and a waste of everyone’s time.”
“PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS,” says Judah Mann of New York. “Oh, wait, you already did. Ok, I’m out.”
Or as Naomi from California puts it: “I am sad that AI has breached the one online resource I truly love.”
Because I enjoy the irony, I scraped the 171 comments left on the Times’ announcement and asked Codex (running GPT-6.1 Sol, at medium thinking) to do some sentiment analysis. (Twelve of the 171 were comments left by Times staffers; I’m excluding them here.) Roughly 77% of the reader comments were negative about the new AI features, it found, versus 14% positive and the remainder neutral or mixed. Among the biggest categories of complaint: This shouldn’t require AI. AI is destroying the environment. AI is not why I’m paying the Times $390 a year. The adjustments the AI produces are going to be bad.
Dozens of commenters asked for a way to turn off the feature. “No, not at this time,” Ko responded, “though this feature is completely optional to use.” Indeed: Don’t ask AI to substitute your chard and AI won’t substitute your chard.
One consistent thread was that cooking is supposed to present you with difficulties and challenges and the whole point is figuring them out by yourself. “Anyone using AI for cooking has no sense of taste and no desire to work out the intricacies of cooking and baking,” writes Michael King from Brooklyn. “To use AI for recipes is beyond the pale. If you are going to use AI, then just cut to the chase and defenestrate yourself.” Or BJ from North Carolina: “So, you’re telling me that I’m too stupid to figure it out on my own?”
Meanwhile, the few positive comments tended to focus on how the AI feature had, in fact, made dietary substitutions easier for them. “I love the new AI feature because it quickly (and so far) accurately converts recipes to gluten free,” Anne Wagner from Kansas City writes. “I don’t cook for stress relief,” says Andy from San Francisco. “I cook to put dinner on the table. Anything that makes the process a little faster or smoother is welcome.”
NotesOlives, yecch. ↩There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.” ↩

articles.sourceTitle: Microsoft and Epic Games Suddenly Agree That AI Is Theft
articles.title: Microsoft And Epic Games Suddenly Agree That AI Is Theft
articles.text:
The past four weeks have been something of a wake-up call for the video game industry. You’ve read the headlines, so you know the deal by now: AI advancements spearheaded by Claude Opus 5.5 have turned the world of coding on its axis. Decompilations that used to take months, or even years, are now being pumped out on a daily basis, and publishers can’t keep up with the deluge of vibe-coded browser ports and “native” PC recompilations. I’ve been covering and researching this over the past month, and there’s one recurring topic that keeps popping up in every comment section I read: karma. For many, this is the video game industry’s “you reap what you sow” moment, proof that the AI tools many publishers have brazenly admitted to using are a double-edged sword. It’s a tricky subject to tackle, because it comes packaged alongside so much bias. For instance, where the PlayStation emulation scene is concerned, many see it as retribution for Sony’s decision to kill physical media. Nintendo has maintained a mostly ambivalent stance on generative AI, yet some consider the explosion in vibe-coded recomps as punishment for the company’s litigious history. However, there’s a less ambiguous side to this discussion that I’m far more interested in tackling: hypocrisy. Many publishers are gleefully and very publicly advertising their use of AI to develop games, yet two specific publishers are attempting to have their cake and eat it too in this respect: Microsoft and Epic Games.

Hundreds of DMCA notices have been fired off by companies in response to the recent flood of AI-powered recomps. Indie games are the prime targets, with takedown notices for open-sourced versions of Mega Crit’s Slay the Spire 2, Maddy Makes Games’ Celeste, and Ludeon Studios’ RimWorld all featuring in GitHub’s DMCA logs over the past four weeks. These three examples are important to note because they are blameless victims of vibe-coding: games that feature no generative AI content, yet have been open-sourced against their developers’ wishes.

On the other hand, Epic Games issued a DMCA notice against a vibe-coded browser port of Fortnite on October 10, and Microsoft has issued multiple DMCA notices for Minecraft, Call of Duty, and Halo-related web browser ports over the past month. I could fill this article with dozens of examples of Microsoft’s and Epic Games’ love of AI, but here are two off the dome: Epic Games’ vibe-coded shitshow of a launcher that launched on October 14, and the mere existence of Microsoft’s Copilot.  Epic Games took down a recent project that allowed Fortnite (recreation) to be playable through a web browser.  They also DMCA (copyright) almost every post featuring it LMFAOO pic.twitter.com/7lSK4QksBk — Backers (@BackersGamesF) October 14, 2026  Here’s a fun quote from Tim Sweeney in an interview with PC Gamer: “It’s unfortunate that so many of the AI companies operating early on had such shitty practices, you know, like one of them was found by a court to have gone off to a BitTorrent site and downloaded terabytes of data. That’s ridiculous, they shouldn’t do that.” There’s an interesting use of the past tense here; AI companies had “such shitty practices,” not have. It’s almost as if he thinks this stolen data has been scrubbed and won’t recursively be used to continue training AI models or something. But AI remains built on theft, and no major AI companies have yet been forced to engage in model disgorgement, a legal remedy that forces AI companies to delete all models built on stolen data.

Also note that Sweeney neglects to mention the exact AI company he’s referring to; he simply says that “one of them” was found to have used “a BitTorrent site” to train itself. As PC Gamer notes, Epic’s artists use both Google Gemini’s Nano Banana and OpenAI’s GPT Image. Both Google Gemini and OpenAI are involved in ongoing lawsuits that allege the scraping of materials from piracy sites. However, PC Gamer’s interview with Sweeney is from June 2026. Let’s give Epic the benefit of the doubt and assume they’ve moved on to an AI model that wasn’t built on stolen data. According to an October 12 report from Bloomberg, Epic Games’ upcoming “AI first” Disney/Marvel game will be developed using Anthropic’s Claude. In September 2025, Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5 billion for training its models using illegally obtained data sourced from BitTorrent. However, while Anthropic was forced to delete the stolen data, it was not forced to delete or rework the models it had trained on said data. Meanwhile, Epic Games’ Terms of Service specifically states that you “may not[…]use code or content extracted from the Licensed Products as training input for any Generative AI Program or as prompt-based input where the Generative AI Program trains on input data.” It seems Epic Games is happy to use AI models trained on stolen data, but it’s not happy for anyone else to train AI models on their stuff.

And now, on to Microsoft—and honestly, where do you even begin here? Probably with the $80 billion per year the company has committed to building AI data centers. I guess that sum explains why Activision just had to use AI to generate in-game artwork for both Call of Duty: Black Ops 6 and Call of Duty: Black Ops 7. After all, if they didn’t save a few pennies by generating some AI slop, how would Microsoft’s shareholders know they’re getting their money’s worth? Speaking of Call of Duty, did you notice how many vibe-coded CoD web ports were wiped from the internet via DMCA notices over the past month? I count at least six. To be fair, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma stated the company “remain[s] committed” to “being responsible stewards of IP” in her Xbox Labs announcement on October 13, so I guess we shouldn’t be surprised.  Today we're standing up XBOX LABS (https://t.co/wzXPNnCmI6). Here is the note that I sent to the team: Team,
The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to… — ASHA (@asha_shar) October 13, 2026  But let’s be honest for a second: “being responsible stewards of IP” isn’t Microsoft’s modus operandi. “Responsible” is just a cute buzzword to throw in here, as it implies that the company gives a shit about everyone else’s IP, too. Funny, considering that time Microsoft’s Senior Product Manager suggested users use a “well-known dataset”—all seven Harry Potter books—to “generate new AI-driven Harry Potter fan fiction.”

That’s just a one-off example, though. It’s not like Brent Hecht, Microsoft’s director of applied sciences, stated that the scraping the internet by LLMs represents the “largest theft of labor in human history” or anything, right? In case you didn’t know, The New York Times is currently suing both Microsoft and OpenAI, and Hecht’s comments were obtained during discovery. “Millions of people around the world will soon consider large models ‘hoovering up’ all their work to be an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions,” stated Hecht. “Almost no one intended for content they created to be used in this fashion, nor are they compensated for its use.” There’s a depressingly humorous quote in there too, sourced directly from Microsoft’s internal communications: a warning that generative AI could “significantly disrupt the employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained.” “Our AI content strategy has started a ‘doom loop’ that will hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time,” stated another internal Microsoft memo. “It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers, but that is the situation we have created for our LLM business with respect to its ‘content supply chain.’” Did you also know that Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella, along with Vice Chair and President Brad Smith, have suddenly become very concerned with tighter AI regulations over the past month? Brad thinks it’s worrying that “your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI,” and Nadella now believes that an “authorized person” should be able “to pause or shut down a model mid-task.” Are these quotes related to web browser ports of Microsoft IPs? Not specifically, but it’s awfully funny that they’re changing their tune now that AI is empowering individuals to commit IP theft. Guess it’s fine when they do it, though!

Let me be clear: I don’t think it should be legal for you to vibe-code ports of Fortnite and Call of Duty, and I’m certainly not against better AI regulations. As much as I’m enjoying seeing them get a taste of their own medicine, I’m not advocating for you to rip off the big corps. I’m not asking you to “leave the billion-dollar company alone”—to be frank, I couldn’t give less of a fuck if Microsoft and Epic Games’ profit margins dip. But AI’s ability to recompile games isn’t hurting the big guys; it’s hurting indie games. AAA publishers can just throw lawyers at this over and over again, but for indie developers who self-publish their own games, such efforts would burn a sizable hole in the company account.

I would be a hypocrite if I advocated for vibe-coded theft, which hurts indie developers more than it does billion-dollar companies. This article isn’t in defense of Microsoft and Epic Games; it’s in support of Mega Crit, Maddy Makes Games, Ludeon Studios, and every indie dev out there that’s suddenly too afraid to publish their demos on Steam. You didn’t invest in the stealing machine. You didn’t use AI to cut corners. You didn’t agree to this. You have my sympathy. Update 10/27/2026, 10:03 a.m. ET: Epic Games’ Tim Sweeney has responded to the points raised in this article in a post on X. Sweeney stated that it “conflates a number of different things” and offered a “breakdown” of the “separate components of what is happening” in reply.

Sweeney conceded that Epic Games does not “let people use [the] Fortnite IP without permission or compensation” and confirmed that it does indeed “restrict AI training on outputs of Unreal Engine and MetaHuman,” but stated that the company is “working to remove this restriction from EULA terms.”  This conflates a number of different things. Here is a breakdown of the separate components of what is happening – – Does Epic let people use Fortnite IP without permission or compensation? No. – Does Epic restrict AI training on outputs of Unreal Engine and MetaHuman? Yes… — Tim Sweeney (@TimSweeneyEpic) October 27, 2026  However, Sweeney also pushed back on the grey legal area around Epic Games’ use of Anthropic’s Claude: “What does the law say about the copyright issues associated with training on content? The Anthropic court ruling found they were liable for copyright infringement when torrenting pirated content (as the article quotes me on), but they found that the training itself was fair use. Other courts have found that whether particular content produced by AI was infringing dependent on its similarity to the copyrighted work.” Kotaku has reached out to Tim Sweeney via Epic Games’ Communications team for further comment.
